title: Class AI Risk Audit (Lab)
summary: Groups act as a class safety board, auditing an anonymised AI use-log against the rules, ranking the gaps on a likelihood-impact matrix, and proposing one rule to fix the top-priority risk.
objectives: Audit the class's own AI use against a responsible-use rule set and propose one improvement.
Rank risks by likelihood and impact on a simple risk matrix and choose which to mitigate first.
Write one responsible-use rule to close a gap found in the audit.

sections.heading: Class AI Risk Audit (Lab)
body: Today your group becomes a class safety board. You will audit how AI has actually been used, rank the risks you find, and decide which one to fix first - then write the rule that fixes it.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can audit our AI use against a rule set and find a gap.
I can place risks on a matrix by likelihood and impact.
I can propose one rule to reduce the highest-priority risk.

terms.definition: Checking real practice against a set of rules to find gaps.
How often a risk could happen.
How much harm a risk would cause.
To reduce a risk, often by adding a rule.
A place where practice does not meet the rule.

sections.heading: Audit against the rules
body: An [[audit]] compares what actually happened with what should happen. You read the anonymised class use-log and flag any entry that breaks or stretches a responsible-use rule.
The log is anonymised on purpose: you fix systems and habits, *never* blame a person.

sections.heading: Rank, then rule
body: Place each flagged risk on the matrix by its [[likelihood]] and [[impact]], then pick the highest-priority one.
Finally, write one realistic responsible-use rule that would close that gap - and be ready to pitch it for the class charter.

sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Audit the anonymised use-log, flag the gaps, plot the risks on the matrix, and propose one rule to fix the top-priority risk.
items: Read each log entry against the rule set.
Flag gaps and name the risk and who it affects.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which risk surprised you as higher priority than expected?
How do you make a rule strong but still realistic?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write one change you will make to your own AI use after this audit.
Explain why anonymising the log matters.

worksheet.title: Week 5 - Lab - Worksheet | Class AI Risk Audit (Lab)

questions.prompt: Your group is the class safety board. Put the five audit steps into the order you carry them out.

items.text: Plot each flagged risk on the likelihood-impact matrix.
Read each log entry against the rule set.
Write and pitch one rule that would close the gap.
Flag the gaps and name the risk and who it affects.

feedback.correct: That is the audit order - you can only rank risks you have found, and you only write a rule once you know which risk comes first.
feedback.incorrect: An audit compares practice with the rules first. Ranking comes after flagging, and the rule is written for the risk you circled.

questions.prompt: Which of these entries in the anonymised class use-log are genuine gaps your board should flag?

options.text: A demo prompt was typed in with a student's full name still in it.
An AI answer about rainfall was pasted into a report without being checked anywhere else.
A class photo was uploaded to a tool to turn it into a cartoon poster.
A student asked the teacher whether a new app was safe before using it.
A student checked an AI fact against the textbook before putting it in their work.

feedback.correct: Yes - a gap is a place where practice does not meet the rule, and identifying data or unchecked output are exactly that.
feedback.incorrect: Asking an adult and checking a fact against a trusted source are the rules being followed, not gaps - the gaps are the names, the photo and the unchecked answer.

questions.prompt: Match each flagged risk to where it belongs on the likelihood-impact matrix.

left.text: Real names are typed into prompts in most lessons, and a named student could be exposed to strangers.
An AI sentence is copied into a personal rough draft most weeks, and nobody but the writer ever reads that draft.
One unchecked AI statistic has been printed once all year - in the newsletter sent to every family.
A tool once mis-spelled a group's name on a practice slide, which was deleted a minute later.

feedback.correct: Well placed - likelihood is how often it could happen and impact is how much harm it would cause, and they are judged separately.
feedback.incorrect: Judge the two axes one at a time: how often does it happen, and how much harm does it do when it does? Something frequent can still be low impact.

questions.prompt: Your board has plotted these four risks on the likelihood-impact matrix. Which one should the class mitigate first?

options.text: The unchecked statistic in the newsletter, because it reached every family.
Real names typed into prompts, because it happens often and a named student could be exposed.
AI sentences copied into private rough drafts, because it happens most weeks.
The mis-spelled group name, because it is the one everybody noticed.

feedback.correct: Right - the risk that is high on both axes is the one to mitigate first, not the one that is merely frequent or merely serious.
feedback.incorrect: Compare both axes. The newsletter is serious but rare, the rough drafts are frequent but harmless - only the names are high on likelihood and impact.

questions.stem: Before any prompt is typed, replace every real name with the words '___'. This closes the gap because identifying data is never entered, so the ___ of a student being exposed drops.

feedback.correct: That is a realistic mitigation - swapping the name keeps the prompt useful while moving the risk down the likelihood axis.
feedback.incorrect: A workable rule keeps the task possible: use a general word like 'a student' instead of a real name, which makes exposure far less likely.

formative.targets: Directly checks 'recognises basic risks (incorrect outputs, unsafe use)'
formative.check: Completed audit sheet with a matrix-placed priority risk and a proposed mitigation rule
formative.successCriteria: Finds a genuine gap, places risks sensibly on the matrix, and proposes a realistic rule that reduces the top risk.
formative.evidence: Audit sheet and risk matrix photo.
